blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights the Pretzel paper as a significant contribution to the debate on end-to-end encryption versus provider-supplied functions (e.g., spam filtering) in email systems. The authors demonstrate that it is feasible to achieve both end-to-end encryption and provider functions without prohibitive overheads, challenging the status quo where emails are exposed in plaintext to mail servers. Pretzel achieves this through a combination of end-to-end encryption and secure two-party computation (2PC), enabling providers to perform classification tasks (e.g., spam filtering, topic extraction) on encrypted emails without learning their contents. The paper also explores modern cryptographic building blocks like Yao garbled circuits and homomorphic encryption, showing how these can be combined to make such systems practical. While the paper focuses on email, the techniques are broadly applicable to other domains where privacy-preserving computation is desired.
paper_title: Pretzel: Email Encryption and Provider-Supplied Functions Are Compatible
paper_abstract: Emails today are often encrypted, but only between mail servers— the vast majority of emails are exposed in plaintext to the mail servers that handle them. While better than no encryption, this arrangement leaves open the possibility of attacks, privacy violations, and other disclosures. Publicly, email providers have stated that default end-to-end encryption would conflict with essential functions (spam filtering, etc.), because the latter requires analyzing email text. The goal of this paper is to demonstrate that there is no conflict. We do so by designing, implementing, and evaluating Pretzel. Starting from a cryptographic protocol that enables two parties to jointly perform a classification task without revealing their inputs to each other, Pretzel refines and adapts this protocol to the email context. Our experimental evaluation of a prototype demonstrates that email can be encrypted end-to-end and providers can compute over it, at tolerable cost: clients must devote some storage and processing, and provider overhead is roughly 5× versus the status quo.
